questions.promptText: As shown in the figure, a ball falls freely and contacts a light vertical spring directly below, compressing it until the ball’s speed is zero. Which statement about the ball’s motion after contact is correct?

options.text: After contact, the ball decelerates with the magnitude of acceleration increasing while the speed decreases to zero
The point where speed is zero and acceleration is zero is the position of maximum compression
After contact, the ball first accelerates and then decelerates; its speed first increases, then decreases to zero
The position of maximum speed is the position of maximum compression

questions.explanation: Initially, with little compression, the spring force F < mg, so the net force is downward and the ball accelerates. When F = mg, the net force is zero, so the acceleration is zero and the speed is at its maximum. With further compression, F > mg, the net force is upward, and the ball decelerates until v = 0 at the position of maximum compression, where the upward acceleration is largest in magnitude. Hence (A) is wrong because the ball first accelerates, (B) is wrong because a ≠ 0 at maximum compression, (C) is correct, and (D) is wrong because maximum speed occurs at F = mg, not at maximum compression.

questions.promptText: A wind tunnel uses smoke particles to visualize airflow. The trajectory of a smoke particle is the curve shown. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The smoke particle has constant velocity
The smoke particle must undergo uniformly accelerated curvilinear motion
The acceleration at P could point horizontally to the left
The net force at Q could point vertically downward

questions.explanation: Curvilinear motion changes the direction of velocity, so the velocity vector necessarily varies — (A) is wrong. Uniformly accelerated curvilinear motion requires a constant net force (such as projectile motion); an arbitrary curved trajectory does not generally satisfy this — (B) is wrong. At P , the curve is concave (centre of curvature above P ), so the centripetal component of the acceleration has an upward component; the total acceleration cannot be purely horizontal-leftward — (C) is wrong. At Q, near the crest of the curve, the tangent is roughly horizontal. If the tangential acceleration is zero there, the net force points along the centripetal direction, i.e., vertically downward — (D) is possible.
